extracted.intended_audience: federal agencies, human resources and legal practitioners, policy stakeholders, and commenters on OPM rulemaking regarding civil service classifications
extracted.subtask_short: OPM Schedule F final rule response
extracted.subtask_description: A government final-rule response-to-comments explaining OPM's interpretation of title 5 provisions (e.g., 5 U.S.C. 2302, 3302, 7511), precedent, and the predicted impacts of Executive Order 13957 / Schedule F on adverse action rights, recruitment, politicization, whistleblowing, and related civil service protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 5 U.S.C. 2302(a)(2)(B) (covered position)
rubrics_metrics.description: Positions excepted from the competitive service because of their “confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating character” are excluded from protections against prohibited personnel practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM construes this statutory language as aligning with reasoning about chapter 75: such positions have long been understood to be political appointees and, in addition to not having adverse action rights, are not covered by protections against prohibited personnel practices. (text: “positions of a ‘confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating’ character have long been understood to be political appointees… are not covered by protections against prohibited personnel practices.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Presidential authority under 5 U.S.C. 3302
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may except positions from the competitive service where “conditions of good administration warrant,” but that authority relates to excepting positions, not removing incumbents' previously accrued adverse action rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM: Section 3302 pertains to whether positions should be excepted from the competitive service; Congress did not indicate the same standard should be used to strip incumbents' civil service protections under chapter 75. The rule does not change Presidential authority to except positions, but OPM disagrees that section 3302 allows removal of accrued adverse action rights. (text: “Section 3302 and the ‘warrant[ed]’ ... relates to whether positions should be excepted... Congress did not suggest ... that the same standard also be used in determining whether to remove civil service protections for the incumbents.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of 5 U.S.C. 7511(b)(2) (exception cannot remove accrued adverse action rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: The exception in 5 U.S.C. 7511(b)(2) cannot be read to remove previously accrued adverse action rights of incumbents of positions moved to an excepted schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM's position: incumbents retain accrued rights; historic practice shows employees moved to excepted service retained rights they had accrued. The agency disagrees with broad readings that would nullify accrued procedural protections. (text: “OPM does not believe the exception in 5 U.S.C. 7511(b)(2) can remove the previously accrued adverse action rights of the incumbents of such positions.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent limits (Free Enterprise Fund and Arthrex not general authorization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme Court cases like Free Enterprise Fund and Arthrex provide narrow remedies for unique statutory schemes and do not authorize wholesale removal of civil service protections from career employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free Enterprise Fund addressed multi-layered removal protections for certain independent-agency officers and crafted narrow remedies; it explicitly declined to cast doubt on civil service usage in agencies generally. Arthrex similarly fashioned a limited remedial solution for APJs. These cases do not support removing accrued adverse action rights from thousands of career civil servants. (text summarizing cases and OPM's conclusion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical meaning of ‘confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating’
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase has historically been understood to describe noncareer political appointees, not career civil servants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress, courts, and the Federal Government have parsed this term of art over at least 90 years and consistently viewed it as applying to noncareer political appointees. Executive Order 13957 was the departure from that history. (text: “they have, except in Executive Order 13957, always meant noncareer political appointees.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of moving employees to excepted service on accrued rights
rubrics_metrics.description: When competitive service employees have been involuntarily moved to excepted service schedules, those incumbents have historically kept accrued rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM cites precedent (e.g., Roth v. Brownell) and historical practice indicating incumbents retain rights they accrued prior to the move. Thus transferring positions does not automatically nullify accrued procedural protections. (text: “competitive service employees have in the past been moved involuntarily ... but those incumbents have kept rights they have accrued.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for clear limiting principles and definitions for exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions to civil service protections must have clear limiting principles; vague, broad definitions (e.g., of ‘policy-making’) risk swallowing protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argued Schedule F lacked limiting principles and could be interpreted to cover many levels of employees (examples: agencies petitioning to place 68% of its workforce; spreadsheet labeling GS-? attorneys as policy). OPM agrees concerns about breadth and lack of meaningful boundary: without clear definitions, scope is indeterminate. (text: concerns about Schedule F's ‘no limiting principle’ and indeterminate scope up to 250,000 employees.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of recruitment, hiring, and retention impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking should consider evidence of how politicization or removal of protections will affect recruitment, hiring, and retention, especially for technical and cybersecurity positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM received significant comments and academic research that politicization deters applicants (including IT/technical). Examples: technical roles require maintenance of confidences; evidence from commenters and Section V(B) describing negative impacts. Decisions should be grounded in evidence, not mere assertions that conversion to at-will would be harmless. (text: “OPM received a significant number of comments concerned about the negative impacts ... on recruitment.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of politicization risks to merit system principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals must be assessed for whether they inject politicization into the merit-based civil service and thus run counter to merit system principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM's rule is based on determination that injecting politicization into the nonpartisan career civil service (or creating conditions where it can be injected) would harm employees, agencies, services, and the public. Commenters argued Schedule F could be used for partisan retribution. (text: “injecting politicization ... runs counter to merit system principles ... and would not only harm government employees... but also the American people.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance management justification standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A schedule/exemption justified as a performance-management tool must demonstrably address performance problems; converting employees based on job characteristics (e.g., work on policy) does not target poor performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM found Schedule F poorly designed for improving performance; it sought to streamline terminations based on type of work, not on how well someone performs. Existing statutory tools and processes (chapter 75, chapter 43, probationary removals, civil rights adjudication) already address performance/misconduct. The appropriate solution is legal/regulatory reform or proper use of existing tools, not an executive order undermining statutory protections. (text: “the characteristics of an employee's job—including whether the employee works on policy—has nothing to do with an employee's performance.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process and appealability consequences of making employees at-will
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting positions to at-will status removes procedural safeguards like written notice, opportunity to respond, and appealability for adverse actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An at-will employee might not have entitlement to written notice of reasons for adverse action, opportunity to respond, or a written decision, and decisions generally would not be appealable; thus it becomes difficult to detect or remedy politically-motivated actions. (text: “it would be, at a minimum, difficult for employees to protect themselves ... because no cause (or evidence) would be required prior to such an action.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Burrowing-in risk and requirements for merit-based hiring
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule changes should be evaluated for their potential to enable 'burrowing in'—political appointees moving into permanent career positions without competition or merit-based selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM requires politics play no role in hiring for career jobs and reviews appointments; Executive Order 13957 could have opened the door for moving political appointees into Schedule F positions or transferring vacancies without competition, increasing burrowing risk even if hires are at-will. (text: “Executive Order 13957... could have opened the door for agency heads to move current political appointees ... without competition ... allowing political appointees ... to ‘burrow’ into permanent civil service appointments.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Whistleblower protections preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy changes must consider effects on whistleblower protections; removal from competitive service could undermine ability to prove retaliation for protected disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argued Schedule F could give the President discretion to cancel the Whistleblower Protection Act by removing employees from the competitive service and firing them at will, making it difficult to prove removal was due to protected whistleblowing. Also, excluded positions might no longer be ‘covered positions’ under prohibited personnel practices. (text: concerns from Comment 3340 and others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Impacts on separation of powers and legislative authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether actions would weaken legislative power or upset constitutional checks and balances by increasing executive control over career personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argued Schedule F frustrates the institutional design of checks and balances and weakens legislative power; OPM notes the Founders' concerns with centralized power and that such changes implicate core institutional design. (text: “the Founders were deeply concerned with the amassing of centralized power, and Schedule F frustrates the institutional design of checks and balances.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of shifting work to contractors and data/trust consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether policy changes would increase reliance on private contractors, raising costs and diminishing public trust in government-curated data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argued Schedule F would likely increase contractor reliance (more expensive) and could erode trust in scientific/economic data curated by career civil servants free from political influence, resulting in social value loss. (text: “a likely consequence ... would be a greater reliance on private contractors ... more expensive ... data is trusted precisely because it is curated by career civil servants who are free from political influence.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing statutory/regulatory mechanisms (probation, chapters 43 & 75, civil rights processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before creating new exceptions, consider using or reforming existing mechanisms (probationary removals, chapter 75/43 procedures, EEO processes) that already address misconduct and performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM notes existing tools remove many poor performers annually, probation serves as job filtering for new appointees, and civil rights statutes and EEO adjudication remain available even if positions were excepted. Creating Schedule F would not prevent constitutional or statutory claims and could result in more litigation. (text: multiple paragraphs on probation, existing removals, and civil rights adjudications.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for empirical evidence and avoiding cherry-picking/anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory changes should be supported by rigorous evidence; anecdotal or cherry-picked examples are insufficient to justify broad removal of protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment 2822 criticized ‘Tales from the Swamp’ for cherry-picking and slanted interpretation; the most thorough report found many agency losses in court were due to unlawful political actions by appointees, not career staff sabotage. OPM emphasizes reliance on substantiated evidence rather than anecdotes. (text: critique that anecdotes lack context and do not justify reorienting the civil service.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for veterans' preference and statutory hiring requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Merit-based hiring procedures and protections like veterans' preference are statutory; concerns about their effects should be addressed to Congress rather than bypassed by executive actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM notes many ‘difficulties’ arise from statutory veterans' preference and that removing or evading such legal requirements via executive action is inappropriate; legislative change is the route for reform. (text: “If a commenter believes they ‘make it difficult to hire the best candidates’ the solution is to make this argument to Congress… the merit-based hiring procedures are one of the ways agencies can defend themselves from unsupported assertions of illegal discrimination.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification and assessment of scope (how many positions affected)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule evaluations must quantify likely scope: how many positions and what GS/levels would be covered, and whether agency interpretations could vastly expand coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters provided estimates (e.g., 4,000 political positions; 1,000–1,500 Schedule C appointees). Other commenters estimated Schedule F could expand to tens or hundreds of thousands of employees; GAO found agencies interpreted Schedule F broadly (one agency petitioned to place 68% of workforce). OPM highlights indeterminate and potentially expansive scope as a problem. (text: numerical estimates and GAO example.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial doctrine caution: don't hide sweeping changes in vague text (‘no elephants in mouseholes’)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts caution against construing vague statutory provisions as authorizing fundamental changes to regulatory schemes without clear congressional intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPM cites the Supreme Court's warning that Congress does not hide elephants in mouseholes and rejects argument that CSRA quietly allows a President to nullify removal restrictions via vague terms. Major changes to longstanding protections require clear Congressional authorization. (text: “Congress ‘does not hide elephants in mouseholes.’ … that would be contrary to the very purpose of the CSRA.”)
